key_facts: **Milia** are 1–2 mm white **keratin cysts** just under the epidermis.
**Primary**: very common in newborns (nose, cheeks) and on adult eyelids and cheeks.
**Secondary**: after blistering, burns, dermabrasion, or potent topical steroids.
Diagnosis is clinical; look for a cause of secondary milia (e.g. PCT on the backs of the hands).
Reassure; troublesome milia can be de-roofed and expressed; topical retinoids for multiple lesions.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Milia** are 1–2 mm superficial **keratin cysts** (tiny epidermoid cysts). **Primary** milia arise spontaneously (up to half of newborns; also adults on the eyelids and cheeks). **Secondary** milia follow blistering, trauma, burns, dermabrasion or potent topical steroids.

sub: Up to half of newborns have milia; common at all ages.
Milia en plaque: rare plaque of milia, usually behind the ear in middle-aged women.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Primary milia form from the lower **infundibulum of vellus hairs**; secondary milia form when damaged sweat ducts, follicles or epidermis become trapped during healing.

ul: Primary: retention of keratin in the lower infundibulum of vellus hairs.
Secondary: damage to follicles or sweat ducts during blistering or trauma; steroid-induced skin atrophy.
**"They're whiteheads"**: milia are closed cysts without an opening; they do not respond to acne cleansers.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: A milium is a **miniature epidermoid cyst** trapped just under the surface.

mech.t: Keratin made by a tiny follicle or sweat duct cannot escape to the surface.
A sac lined by epidermis fills with layered keratin, seen as a pearly white dot.
mech.caption: Milia: tiny keratin cysts in the upper dermis just beneath the epidermis, seen as white dome papules.

mech.t: When blisters or wounds heal, fragments of epithelium are trapped and form new cysts.

histo: Small cyst with a stratified squamous lining and laminated keratin, like a tiny epidermoid cyst.

ul: Firm, pearly **white or yellow** dome papules, 1–2 mm.
Face (eyelids, cheeks, nose) in primary milia; at sites of previous blisters or scars in secondary milia (e.g. hands in porphyria cutanea tarda or epidermolysis bullosa).
Neonatal milia: nose and cheeks; resolve within weeks.

figs.caption: Periocular milia: tiny firm white keratin cysts around the eyes.
Neonatal milia on the nose and cheeks; they clear without treatment.
Secondary milia after blistering (here pemphigoid) — a clue to a past subepidermal blister.

sub: Often with Epstein pearls in the mouth; reassure, resolves in weeks.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical. Dermoscopy shows a white-yellow globule. Look for a cause of secondary milia (blistering disease, PCT, steroid use).

ul: **Comedones** (acne): central keratin plug in a follicle, other acne lesions.
**Syringoma**: skin-coloured papules on the lower eyelids.
**Sebaceous hyperplasia**: yellow umbilicated papules with crown vessels.
**Molluscum contagiosum**: umbilicated, pearly papules, often in children.
If cosmetically troublesome: de-roofing with a sterile needle and gentle expression (de-roofing and extraction).
Topical retinoids may help multiple milia; avoid potent steroids that provoke them.

ladder.t: Neonatal milia resolve within weeks; many adult milia persist but are harmless.
De-roof with a sterile needle or blade and express the keratin (trained clinician).
Topical retinoid; treat the underlying blistering disease; avoid potent topical steroids on the face.

refer.t: Milia with skin fragility, blisters and scarring on the backs of the hands: investigate for **porphyria cutanea tarda** or epidermolysis bullosa.
Milia en plaque or widespread milia: dermatology.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Milia on scarred, fragile skin of the backs of the hands: think **porphyria cutanea tarda** or epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.
Cosmetic concern only; scarring if picked.
Neonatal milia clear; adult and secondary milia may persist.
Milia are **cysts**, not blocked sebaceous glands; squeezing without de-roofing does not work.

quiz.a: Tiny superficial keratin cysts (miniature epidermoid cysts), 1–2 mm, white.

quiz.q: Name three causes of secondary milia.
quiz.a: Blistering diseases (PCT, EB, pemphigoid), burns or dermabrasion, potent topical steroids.
De-roofing with a sterile needle or blade and gentle expression.
No; they resolve on their own within weeks.
